subsubtopic: CONTROL OF INDUSTRIAL PLANTS AND OIL REFINERIES
speechtext:
for leave to introduce Bill No. 6, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to amend and enlarge sections 19, 26 and 28 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act. When the act was originally passed it prohibited the pollution of navigable waters by saw mills. Section 19 of the original act prohibited the discharging of sawdust or other waste wood products into navigable waters or waters running into them. The proposed amendment enlarges the list of materials which may not be thrown or discharged into navigable waters, so that it will include oil or oil sludge, chemical wastes or other noxious substances likely to pollute the waters and adjacent shore line.
The second clause of this section deals with the discharging of raw sewage into navigable waters. It prohibits any municipality with a population greater than 3,000 from discharging such material.
Section 26 is amended to provide that the Minister of Transport may, if he deems it advisable, appoint inspectors at any plant situated on or near navigable waters, and these inspectors shall have the power to regulate the operation of the plant in this regard, the cost of such inspection to be borne by the plant in question.
The reasons for the amendments to this act are that during the summer of 1949 pollution by oil and the formation of oil slicks created such a hazard to the residents along the shore of lake Ontario that the medical officers of health in Toronto and many other municipalities had to ban the use of the beaches. Thus, in the Toronto area alone, a million people were denied the use of lake Ontario beaches because of the existence of industrial pollution. Whether this was caused by carelessness or otherwise is not important now; the fact remains that large sections of the shore of lake Ontario were made completely unusable. The loss to wild life was considerable, and the damage to shallow-draft and other shipping was extensive. Furthermore the fire danger, particularly in the
congested Toronto harbour area, was increased. Three of the beaches in my own riding of York West were put out of commission for considerable periods, including the beach at New Toronto, where the world champion swimmer, Cliff Lumsden, who subsequently won the marathon swim at the Toronto exhibition, had trained. This destruction of swimming and recreational facilities, particularly, as in this case, during one of the worst heat waves in our history, cannot be tolerated.
I believe it is within the competence of parliament to enact legislation which will safeguard the rights of people who wish to use the waters of our great lakes. The provisions of the bill are directed toward that end.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

CONTROL OF SMOKE AND SOOT FROM ROUNDHOUSES
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. 7, to amend the Railway Act.

subtopic: CONTROL OF SMOKE AND SOOT FROM ROUNDHOUSES
speechtext: I think the hon. member should explain the bill.

subtopic: CONTROL OF SMOKE AND SOOT FROM ROUNDHOUSES
speechtext:
The purpose of the bill is similar to that of the bill I introduced at the last session of parliament. It differs, however, in this way from the previous one: it requires permanent installations of the railway companies to comply with the smoke bylaws of the municipalities in which they are situated. The residual power is still vested in the board of transport commissioners, thus preventing any discrimination against railway companies. It is felt that where a municipality has enacted and enforced an anti-smoke bylaw in order to safeguard the well-being of the people within its boundaries, the railway companies, as well as other industrial plants, should comply with the local regulations. The present act, and the regulations, which were drafted in 1908, allow the emission of smoke and soot into the atmosphere in quantities which are certainly prejudicial to the neighbourhood in which any roundhouse is situated.
Evidence is being collected in York township and the adjacent area of the city of Toronto, and I hope that when the bill comes

Criminal Code
up for second reading the government will allow it to go to the railway committee so that all the facts can be brought out, with a view to adopting this or a similar amendment in order to prevent the present great annoyance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
the first reading of Bill No. 4 (from the Senate) to amend the Criminal Code.
He said: With the permission of the house I should like to set forth the reasons why it is advisable, if it meets with the approval of hon. members, to have this legislation pass through its three readings today. To this end I spoke yesterday to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), and to the leaders of the other parties, or their representatives.
At the last session a Criminal Code amendment bill was brought in covering a large number of sections, some of them contentious. It was not passed. Later this session it is our intention to bring down a further amendment to the Criminal Code containing these contentious sections, but we have taken out from the contentious sections those dealing with the two matters which are covered by this bill from the Senate.
Item No. 1 deals with the amendments necessary in order to adapt the Canadian Criminal Code to Newfoundland, and which are to be passed in consequence of the admission of that province into confederation.
Item No. 2 is an amendment to defer the coming into force of a new part XVI of the Criminal Code. This new part XVI of the Criminal Code was enacted by a previous parliament in legislation passed some time ago. It enacts that there should be substituted for the existing part XVI a new part dealing with the summary trial of indictable offences by police magistrates. That legislation was to come into effect on October 1, 1949, but we have received from the provincial authorities of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario, British Columbia, and my own province of Manitoba, information that their magistrates' courts are not yet organized to administer part XVI in its proposed new form. They have asked that we, by means

of section 8 of the Senate bill now before us, should bring new part XVI into operation, not on October 1, as was originally provided, but by proclamation of the governor general in council. The idea is that they will let us know in due course when they are ready to enforce the new part XVI and then we will put it into effect.
Since these consequential amendments which are introduced in order that the Criminal Code may be brought into effect in Newfoundland, as well as the other matter referred to, are both non-controversial, it was thought there would be no objection on the part of hon. members to having the bill given its three readings today, so that it may be assented to by the governor general and take effect by October 1 next.

I should like to mention just two minor points. Section 3 of the bill contains a provision that the Criminal Code shall be amended to read "in the province of Newfoundland, any judge of a district court," etc. The bills introduced to make the Criminal Code applicable to Alberta and Saskatchewan read "a judge of any district court". Is there any significance in that change?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker-
I think I anticipate the hon. member's point of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

Of course no debate is permitted on first reading of a bill, but I understood that the Minister of Justice was setting forth why he would like the bill to be given all three readings today. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I now move second reading of the bill. Before the motion is dealt with, however, I should like to reply to the question raised by the leader of the opposition.

Order. I would remind hon. members that on second reading it is not customary to discuss the clauses of a bill. That is done when the house goes into committee. The only question that may be discussed on second reading is the principle of the bill, and each hon. member is allowed to speak only once in that debate. The minister who has introduced the bill has the right of a reply.

The Minister of Justice has introduced a bill and has asked for unanimous consent to have it proceeded with. Certainly

at some point the minister should answer minor questions which would have a bearing on the consent which may be given. I do not think there is any substantial objection to his suggestion, but this would seem to be an appropriate time for the minister to explain two minor matters, after which there may be no further comment on the measure. I suggest it might be done more appropriately now than in committee, because we are being asked to agree that this bill be given all readings today. I am sure there will be general agreement, but first we should satisfy ourselves as to these minor matters.

I should think that would be generally acceptable to the house. The minister might like to know what questions are being raised, in order that he may answer them. Perhaps the leader of the opposition would ask his questions now.

The other point is in regard to the procedure under which the first seven sections of this bill will become operative. I understand that a step will have to be taken under the terms of agreement with Newfoundland in order to make these amendments applicable. I should think it would be of interest to hon. members from Newfoundland to know what steps will be taken outside of this bill to bring about that result.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was the second question?
Yes; those are the two points.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as the first question is concerned, I do not think there is any substantial difference in meaning between subsection (iva) as contained in section 3 of the Senate bill, where it says "any judge of a district court", and the language to which the hon. gentleman referred, "a judge of any district court", as used in connection with another province. I might add that the question of the district court judges is still in the course of negotiation, even with regard to their number. Many of them have yet to be appointed, so it may turn on that point; but I do not think there is any difference in substance at all.
With regard to the question of bringing this bill into effect, as I indicated on a previous occasion,-to which I suppose I am not permitted to refer-in dealing with amendments to our statute law consequent upon Newfoundland's entering into confederation, from the beginning there has been the closest co-operation and consultation between the law officers of the Department of Justice and the law officers of Newfoundland, and that will be continued in connection with the application of the Criminal Code. In connection with part XVI, for instance, it is necessary that the Criminal Code should be put
Criminal Code
into effect as soon as possible, but not until the provincial authorities are ready to administer it. In the meantime, of course, the criminal law of Newfoundland remains as it is.

I want to refer to just a few matters on the second reading of this bill, which has come to us from another place. I believe this is the same bill that was before us a short time ago, relating to Newfoundland. At that time, when we were assembled here before Easter, I suggested to the Attorney General (Mr. Garson) that we should have in this house a legal committee to consider this and other similar bills. Some two years ago I asked the hon. gentleman's predecessor, in connection with this very matter of Newfoundland, whether he would consider setting up what they have in the various provinces-a legal committee which would properly consider bills of this kind, of which we have a large number. Some originate in this house; some come from "another place", which is the term they are now applying to the other house of parliament. There were some twenty of these bills during the last session. The provinces have found it a good thing to have such a committee. It goes over these bills; it has the law officers of the crown in attendance; it hears deputations of various kinds representing people interested in these matters.
It must be remembered that large numbers of people are concerned with these legal bills. Look at the fatalities resulting from the fact that we do not have such a committee. Look at the accidents on the highways and level crossings. I understood the minister's predecessor to say he would consider setting up such a committee. Then, as I said, I asked the present minister, who is also the Attorney General of Canada, whether he would consider it, and I thought he said he would. In my opinion such a committee would be a great help to the minister.
I cannot find any record of this bill having been sent to any committee in the other place, but it had summary discussion by three or four members of that chamber, and finally it was passed and sent to this house.
There are two or three things I should like to point out about Newfoundland. Newfoundland has become the tenth province of confederation. At the time, that province was under the jurisdiction of the British parliament and had a commission form of government which governed Labrador as well. Two years ago there was a discussion in this house about Labrador's natural resources- I was on the committee. Until recently Newfoundland had no parliamentary form of government. What is it proposed to give to the tenth province through this bill? It is

Criminal Code
supposed to be dealing with amendments to the Criminal Code, but it deals also with a large number of other matters.
I point out what has been said in the British parliament by Right Hon. Sir Hartley Shawcross. Mr. Churchill asked for law reform, and referred to the fact that of the
40.000	orders in council which had been passed, only three or four had reached finality in the privy council. You have been a great lawyer, Mr. Speaker, and, occupying the high office you do, you must appreciate the fact that no one knows the law contained in those
40.000	orders in council until it is finally decided in the court of last resort. Nearly
80.000	orders in council were passed here during the war.
The Attorney General of the United Kingdom was asked by the leader of the opposition, Mr. Churchill, about the state of the law. He said law reform was needed. Surely Newfoundland is entitled to some law reform. Years ago Canada was granted the right to abolish criminal appeals to the privy council. In the British House of Commons there was a discussion on means of securing finality on law reform. Law reform has been talked about in this country, but we have had no semblance of it. A private member can raise these questions in the house, but that is the end of it. As I said before, there were some
40.000	orders in council passed by the British House of Commons, but no one knew the exact state of the law. No one can be sure of the law until there has been a final determination by the privy council.
This is the sort of law you are giving to Newfoundland. Automatically Newfoundland is being given the laws to which she has been objecting. That is the point to which I am objecting in relation to this bill. I believe the bill should be re-introduced in this house, and a legal committee should be set up to consider it. I want to help the government, and I am giving them a constructive suggestion, namely, to beware of the law that is passed on to the tenth province. It is my understanding that this province has one small jail, and only a small percentage of the population has ever occupied it. I am told that a number of prisons in Great Britain have been closed. What means was used to do this? An opportunity was given offenders to delay the payment of fines.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Dion in the chair.
Sections 1 to 4 inclusive agreed to.

On section 5-Absolute jurisdiction in certain cases.
May I ask the purpose of setting out the cities of Saint John, Fredericton and Moncton in the province of New Brunswick? Have they laws which permit of a different arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not sure that I heard the whole of my hon. friend's question; if I misinterpret it, I hope he will correct me. The purpose of this amendment, as is stated in the explanatory notes, is to extend to Newfoundland the provisions of paragraph (c) of subsection 1 of section 777, whereby magistrates are given absolute jurisdiction, without the consent of the accused, to try certain indictable offences. Such jurisdiction is not as a rule given to magistrates in small centres in certain provinces. It is for this reason that those cities are set forth in subsection (c) of clause 5 of the bill.
There is that difference in New Brunswick, whereby only certain ones are selected?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

How many magistrates are there in Newfoundland now, and how many is it proposed to have? Powers are given to magistrates which, with all due respect, I believe should not be given. The jurisdiction granted by this section is rather wide; it permits a magistrate to try grave offences. In England I believe the maximum sentence a magistrate can give is thirty days.
By this bill you are giving a magistrate all the powers of a county court judge. According to the marginal notes, the purpose of the amendment is to extend to Newfoundland the provisions of paragraph (c) of subsection (1) of section 777, whereby magistrates are given absolute jurisdiction, without the consent of the accused, to try certain indictable offences. It is my belief that magistrates in Ontario should not have this jurisdiction. Some grave cases are brought before magistrates, most of whom are not like the late Colonel Denison, who was senior magistrate, and the late Judge Morson, who presided over the first and tenth division courts. There are four or five county court judges doing the work Judge Morson used to do in the first and tenth division court. I object to conferring this jurisdiction upon magistrates in Newfoundland. It will necessitate the maintenance of a huge system which that province does not need. A county court judge could do this work.
I object to the system that is now operated in the city of Toronto, whereby magistrates, instead of trying a case and rendering a decision, merely remand the accused into

custody for a week. There is no place to put the accused. The Don jail and the isolation hospital are located in my constituency. For many years attempts have been made to have them removed. The city of Toronto built two jail farms, one for men and one for women, and at that time it was never intended they should be handed over to anyone else. When I was in charge of the affairs of the city, these two farms were built and the old jail was to be torn down, but it is still there, as hon. members know. I should like the minister to see it. About 400 people are in there; some of them are youths, and some are older. Under the system followed by some of the magistrates, where they remand a man for a week or two weeks, they allow him to get a taste of what the jail is like over there. It was built shortly after confederation. It was condemned when I was a controller. Dr. Hastings, a former health officer, said it was not fit for human beings. It has cell accommodation which is no larger than about the width of this table. It is equipped to handle only about 180 persons, and there are three or four hundred there now. I am objecting to that situation. When Mr. Hepburn was premier of the province he would not allow us to qualify for the fund which was in existence in your province, Mr. Chairman, under which the dominion gave a grant for public buildings. Three Rivers obtained a courthouse. We did not get anything. I ask the minister to consider carefully before he fastens this system on the people of Newfoundland-who have always been law-abiding-without their consent.
Is it the idea held by the law officers that there will be what we call travelling stipendiaries, or something of the kind? I am speaking of the quality of the people who will be giving judgment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. Newfoundland had a system of magistrates prior to coming into confederation. At the request of the attorney general of Newfoundland we at this moment have an officer of the Department of Justice conferring with the attorney general's department in Newfoundland with regard to the judicial system by means of which the Criminal Code will be administered in that province. While it has not yet definitely taken shape, and the purpose of this consultation is to determine its main outlines, it is thought that it will take the form in part of magistrates who will be located at various central points and travel out from these points to hear cases.
Criminal Code
As I have no doubt they have been in the past, these will be men of good judgment and discretion, well qualified to exercise jurisdiction under section 777. This section, as the hon. member for Calgary West knows, deals with indictable offences such as theft, attempted theft, aggravated assault and indecent assault which, in larger centres only in some provinces, in the whole province in others, and not at all in other provinces, can be tried by the magistrates without the consent of the accused. This law has been applicable, in varying degrees, in all the provinces of Canada up until the present time. The only significance and the only purpose of this present amendment is simply to apply to Newfoundland this same law that has always been in force in the rest of Canada; it is not to make any alteration in the law. Magistrates or other judicial officers who are not competent to deal with cases of this kind will not be appointed.

I agree entirely with what the minister has in mind. From the little I know about the settlement of Newfoundland, it is largely along the sea-coast. The thought occurred to me that perhaps travelling stipendiaries might be appointed. They have them in Saskatchewan, I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I thought perhaps we could expect that that would be done.
Having regard to what is probably in the mind of the hon. member for Broadview, I was wondering about the limitation there might be on giving what is really very wide authority to a magistrate-because tremendous authority is given in this section. As I remember it, a magistrate is defined in the code as having the power of two justices of the peace, and I think there is a further definition which in certain cases does not permit those two justices of the peace to act, but rather a paid magistrate so to speak, who is generally a man with legal training; only to him would go cases of the kind we are now referring to. It would be a desperate thing, it seems to me, if we clothed an incompetent, or, to use a less unkind word, untrained person with the tremendous authority which is given there.
As will be observed, wounding is one of the offences dealt with, or assault occasioning actual bodily harm-one or the other. I know there is a distinction between the two, and I do not remember which one is within the offences dealt with; but serious offences come to them for hearing. It seems to me, in view of the spirit of comity which no doubt exists between the dominion justice

Criminal Code
officers and those of the provinces, consideration might be given to having travelling stipendiaries; otherwise you must take the prisoner all over the country, adding to the difficulties, to say nothing of the expense. I hope that is what is contemplated here, so that inconvenience may not be caused to many people other than the accused-and he is probably entitled to be discommoded at times.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am in a rather embarrassing position to forecast what will happen because this whole matter is now under consideration. I believe there is an excellent prospect, shall I say, of appointment being made of the kind of magistrate that the hon. member for Calgary West has in mind. He will see in the bill the definition of magistrate for the purpose of part XVI of the code; it is at the top of page 2. It reads:
In the province of Newfoundland a magistrate means and includes any judge of a district court,-
I am sure he would agree that any judge of a district court would be competent to try these cases.
-any stipendiary magistrate, any two justices sitting together, and any functionary or tribunal having the powers of two justices.
It is the last part of it that I was a little bit afraid of.

I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Justice the fact that there seems to be a drastic change, so far as Newfoundland is concerned, in the matter of persons charged with crime and wishing to have a speedy trial. I understand that in the province of Newfoundland all supreme court judges are located at and live in the capital, St. John's. If a person is charged with a crime at a place five or six hundred miles from St. John's where there is a district court judge-I do not know their locations down there, but I know there are some in the country-it would take a long time, I should think, for that person to come in to St. John's in order to get a speedy trial. I should like the Minister of Justice to give some consideration to this matter. The suggestion would come better from the lawyers of Newfoundland than from me, but it is just a thought. I am fairly well acquainted with the situation in Newfoundland. It will be inconvenient for criminals-not that we are here to make it convenient for them, but we are here at least to give them speedy trial-it will be inconvenient for those away beyond the bounds of the capital city to get a speedy trial if they can get it only by going before a supreme court judge in St. John's.
The accused is probably in the only jail there is, which is in St. John's.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is one of the most important questions which the representative of the justice department and the representatives of the attorney general's department of Newfoundland are studying at the present time. They are considering how many supreme court and district court judges will be required, and whether they should go on circuit for the purpose of conducting speedy trials. It is a matter which requires careful consideration, to balance, on the one hand, the convenience of the accused, and, on the other, in a province where there are great distances, the efficient carrying out, at not too great expense, of the administration of justice.

In Canada a great deal of confusion exists through the use of the term "supreme court." I believe one or two of the provinces have named their courts differently. In order to avoid this confusion, could some arrangement not be made with the provinces to reserve the name "supreme court" for the court of last resort in Canada? Some who speak of the supreme court mean the Supreme Court of Canada, and others mean the supreme court of one of the provinces. We should try to have separate names for the provincial courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid that would be infringing on provincial rights, and for that reason we may not be able to comply with the hon. member's request. Under the British North America Act, the setting up of provincial courts comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
I said by arrangement or agreement.

Section agreed to.
Sections 6 and 7 agreed to.
On section 8-Coming into force.

Early this year I received a copy of a letter from the city council of Vancouver which had been sent by the deputy attorney general of British Columbia to the deputy minister of justice asking for the postponement of this legislation. I would not take the time of the committee to make the point now except for the fact that, by this amendment, the amendment to part XVI is to come into effect by proclamation. This may be a neat way of deferring the provision so that it will never come into effect. The Minister of Justice shakes his head. I take it that that is not what he has in mind. One of the important reasons put forward by the deputy attorney general of British Columbia-and it was also emphasized by the city council of Vancouver-was that if

this amendment went into effect it would result in the loss of revenue to the municipality.
When I received the letter from the city council, with the enclosures, including a copy of the letter to the deputy minister of justice, I did as I always do. Not being learned in the law, I wanted to know what the Minister of Justice said when he introduced the amending legislation in 1948. I have high regard for the then minister of justice, and I would require strong arguments before I would disagree with his conclusions on a matter of this kind. What he said on that occasion was brief, and I made it a part of my letter to the city authorities in Vancouver. He said as reported at page 5193 of Hansard of June 14, 1948:
In part XVI, at the present time magistrates in towns of over 2,500 population have jurisdiction that magistrates in towns under 2,500 do not have. Then there are some provisions for cities over 25,000. At the present time the provisions are very complicated indeed. Continual complaints are made about the necessity to ascertain population of a town or a city, and complaints about magistrates having jurisdiction in certain municipalities. The important change is that under Part XVI at the present time there are indictable offences for which an accused person may be tried by a magistrate, whether he consents or not. He does not have the option of trial by jury. If this amendment is passed, then he could not be tried by a magistrate without his consent. That is an important change.
That is what Mr. Ilsley said in explaining the purpose of this amendment when the bill came before the house. If, as the deputy attorney general of British Columbia maintains, this would mean a loss of revenue to the municipality, surely it is neither here nor there. The important thing is that the accused should have an opportunity of saying how he shall be tried; we should not make our courts the means of raising revenue for the municipality. I said this categorically to the city of Vancouver. As I have watched the imposing of sentences in the courts I have come to the conclusion that when a fine is levied, and it cannot be paid, a prison sentence is imposed, so that really in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred when a person is fined, or given the option of a jail sentence, he is jailed not for the crime but because he is unable to pay the fine. In other words he is jailed for being poor and not for having committed a crime. I urge upon the minister that he see that if this section of the bill is passed it be not used as a convenient way of killing the legislation. If justice is to be meted out, the accused must be taken into consideration, not the revenue that may be gained or lost to the city.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I ask whether, if this section passes, the governor in council will have to wait until all the provinces want to
Criminal Code
have the act proclaimed, or will it be possible to proclaim it for such provinces as are ready for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I should preface my answer to that question by saying that the new part XVI was introduced with the intention that it would come into effect in the ordinary course of events and be the law of the country, and it has been so received by those other provinces. I am told, and I believe, that they have made the best efforts they can to get their house in order so that they can do a good job of administering the new part XVI. Our hope is that with what they have already done they will finally achieve competence to administer the new part XVI. We would not wish to discommode anyone by delay in proclaiming the new part XVI. We are keeping in contact with the provinces and we intend to encourage any provinces that seem to be hanging back in preparing to take over the administration of that part.
Section agreed to.

With the permission of the Minister of Justice I should like to revert to section 5, where reference is made to "the cities of St. John, Fredericton and Moncton in the province of New Brunswick". If my memory serves me correctly, the corporate name of the city of Saint John does not permit any abbreviation such as appears in the subsection. We are jealous of the spelling of the name of our city. In addition, there might be grounds for taking a technical objection. Although a rose by any other name might smell as sweet, we should like to maintain the proper spelling of the name of our city.
Substitute "fish" for "rose" and you have it.
I do not know who was representing my city when the original subsection was passed, but there would seem to be definite evidence of a progressive conservation of print.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. member's point is well taken. I would move that the word "St." be struck out and the word "Saint" substituted therefor.

Amendment agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
I wish to ask the Minister of National Defence a question, of which I have given him notice. Last night

Inquiries of the Ministry and today urgent communications have been coming in to me by telephone and telegram from people who live in Lakeview, Ontario, a heavily populated area in which the Long Branch rifle ranges are located, protesting against the military operations carried out yesterday at the ranges. Heavy explosions are said to have occurred which shook the buildings over a wide section of the area, and dense smoke covered the district. Planes swept low over schools and homes as well. Will the minister make inquiries with a view to protecting the residents of this locality against future occurrences of this kind and give further consideration to changing the location of the ranges to a less populated area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: COMPLAINTS AS TO SMOKE, EXPLOSIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I received notice of this question at quarter to three, not having been in my office when it was delivered. In the time since, I have been able to communicate with two senior officers of the army and air force, as well as a senior civilian official, who were present yesterday when this demonstration took place. Based on those inquiries, which represent the information available to me at this time, I may say it appears that five 3-inch and five 4-2-inch mortar shells were fired in this demonstration. In the opinion of these officials they landed at least three-quarters of a mile from the nearest house.
